title: Your Organs Age at Different Speeds. A New Study Found the Sleep Range That Slows All of Them Down.
excerpt: Columbia researchers built organ-specific aging clocks from brain, heart, lung and immune data. The sweet spot was not eight hours.
body:
Eight hours of sleep has been treated as gospel for decades. A study published in Nature last month says the real number is lower — and the consequences of getting it wrong are written into every organ in your body.

Researchers at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons analysed data from the UK Biobank and built what they call organ-specific aging clocks — statistical models that measure biological aging not across the body as a whole, but organ by organ, using protein data, metabolic markers and brain imaging.

The result: the sleep duration associated with the least accelerated aging across the brain, heart, lungs and immune system falls between 6.4 and 7.8 hours per night. Below six hours, the brain, lungs, heart and immune system all showed signs of faster biological aging. Above eight hours, nearly every organ in the body did.

"Sleep is important in maintaining organ health within a coordinated brain-body network, including metabolic balance and a healthy immune system," said Junhao Wen, the lead researcher and an assistant professor of radiology at Columbia, in a press release.

The finding is significant because it challenges a number most people never thought to question. "I would love to dislodge from the public's collective mentality about sleep that eight hours of sleep is ideal for everyone, or even attainable for everyone," said Dr. Chris Winter, a neurologist and host of the Sleep Unplugged podcast. "The range is essentially an average of seven hours of sleep, not eight."

## Why Organs Age Differently

The study's most novel contribution is the idea that different organs, even within the same person, age at different rates. In the liver, for example, Wen's team built separate aging clocks from protein data, metabolic data and imaging data. Each told a slightly different story.

This organ-level precision matters because it helps explain why some people develop heart disease while others develop cognitive decline, even when their overall health profiles look similar. Sleep, it turns out, may be one of the variables that tips the balance.

Too little sleep was associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, coronary artery disease and gastritis. Too much sleep was linked to those conditions and more, including depression and anxiety. The researchers note that chronically long sleep is often a marker of underlying disease — sleep apnoea, inflammation, neurodegenerative conditions — rather than a cause of harm in itself.

## The South Asian Angle

For the Indian diaspora, the findings arrive at a particularly relevant moment. South Asians already carry elevated baseline risk for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and metabolic syndrome — three of the exact conditions the study links to disordered sleep duration. A 2024 Lancet review estimated that more than 100 million people of South Asian descent worldwide live with type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular mortality in this population runs 40 to 60 per cent higher than in white Europeans matched for age.

That means the margin for error is thinner. What might be a minor risk factor for a European-ancestry individual could be the difference between prevention and disease for a South Asian one. The study's own authors acknowledged this gap: Wen noted that more research is needed involving people of Asian and African descent, since the data came from the UK Biobank, which is heavily weighted toward white European participants.

Dr. Saema Tahir, a board-certified sleep medicine physician in New York, cautioned against treating the range as a rigid prescription. "Sleep is really when the body does its most critical repair work, including cellular restoration, immune regulation, hormonal balance and clearing out metabolic waste from the brain," she said. "What I tell my patients is to use that range as a starting framework, but pay attention to how you feel."

The women in the study needed about 10 to 20 more minutes of sleep than men, likely driven by hormonal fluctuations across the menstrual cycle, pregnancy and menopause.

## What This Means for You

The practical takeaway is not that you should set an alarm for exactly seven hours. It is that the old eight-hour target may be overshooting, and that consistently falling outside the 6.4-to-7.8-hour window is associated with measurable biological costs — costs that compound over years and hit organs individually, not uniformly.

For South Asian diaspora families already managing diabetes, hypertension or heart disease, sleep duration is now one more variable worth tracking — not with anxiety, but with the same attention they give to diet and exercise. The data says seven hours is the centre of gravity. The smartest thing you can do is find out where your body actually falls within it.
